o: Sum the number of distinct characters over all O(n^2) substrings of s. For "abbca" the total is 28. Brute force is far too slow for n = 1e5, so we need a per-character or incremental formulation. Key observation: appending character s[i] to all substrings ending at i increases the appeal by exactly 1 if s[i] did not appear earlier in the substring, i.e., since its previous occurrence.
k: dp[i] = total appeal of all substrings ending at index i = dp[i-1] + (i - last[s[i]]).
Equivalently, each occurrence of a character contributes to substrings starting after its previous occurrence: (i - last) * (n - i).
Only the previous occurrence index of each letter is needed — O(26) state.

a.n: Approach 1: Incremental DP over substring endings
a.i: Maintain cur = sum of appeals of all substrings ending at the current index. When we append s[i], every substring ending here gains 1 appeal iff it starts after the previous occurrence of s[i]; there are i - last[s[i]] such substrings, so cur increases by exactly that amount.
s: Keep last[c] = previous index of letter c (-1 initially) and cur = 0.
For each i: cur += i - last[s[i]]; ans += cur.
a.t: O(n) — single pass with O(1) work per character.

a.i: Instead of tracking substring endings, count directly: character s[i] is the distinct-counted representative for exactly those substrings that start in (last[s[i]], i] and end in [i, n-1], contributing (i - last) * (n - i). Summing over all i gives the same total without a running value.
s: Track last occurrence of each letter.
For each i add (i - last[s[i]]) * (n - i) to the answer.
Update last[s[i]] = i and return the sum.
a.t: O(n) — one pass, constant work per index.

w: Both approaches are linear; the DP version generalizes nicely to 'sum of f(substring)' problems where appending a character changes f predictably. Watch for overflow (use 64-bit) since the answer can reach ~n^2/2. Follow-up: sum of number of distinct characters over subsequences, or k-distinct substring counts.
